context_blurb:
Everything is built from elements, 118 basic substances that cannot be broken into anything simpler. Chemists list them on one chart, the periodic table, and sort them into three families: metals such as gold and iron, nonmetals such as oxygen and sulfur, and metalloids, which fall in between. An element's family tells you how it behaves: whether it shines, bends or shatters, and whether electricity flows through it.

Each element has a symbol of one or two letters, and many come straight from the English name: H for hydrogen, O for oxygen. A few look like a puzzle. Lead is Pb, from plumbum, its name in Latin, the language of ancient Rome; plumbum is also the root of our word plumbing. Iron is Fe from ferrum, silver is Ag from argentum, and gold is Au from aurum. The Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius drew his symbols from the elements' names in Latin around 1814, so that the same letters would stand for an element in every language. Einsteinium, named after Albert Einstein, simply follows its English name: Es.

About four in five elements are metals, so they fill most of the periodic table, from the left side all across the middle, along with the two long rows printed underneath. The nonmetals crowd into the top right corner, all except hydrogen at the top left. The metalloids sit on a zigzag staircase line between the two.

Metals are shiny, carry heat and electricity well, and bend instead of breaking. Gold is the champion of malleability, a metal's power to be hammered or pressed into thin sheets without cracking. A goldbeater can pound a single gram of gold into a sheet about a metre long and a metre wide, so fine that light glows greenish blue through it. Ductility is a close cousin: the power to be drawn out into wire.

Most nonmetals are gases: of the seventeen, eleven are gases at room temperature, among them oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, helium and neon. Bromine is the only liquid, and the other five, among them carbon, sulfur and iodine, are solids. Every metal but mercury is a solid, and so is every metalloid, so every element that is a gas at room temperature is a nonmetal.

Solid nonmetals are mostly dull, they crumble or snap instead of bending, and heat and electricity pass through them poorly. Sulfur, a pale yellow crystal, breaks to crumbs under a hammer and barely carries electricity at all. Like most nonmetals, sulfur sits on the right side of the periodic table, far from the metals. Simple tests like these are how a chemist sorts an element into its family: a look at its shine, a hammer blow and a wire to a battery.

A metalloid usually looks like a metal but acts much like a nonmetal. Germanium shines grey like a metal, yet it is brittle, which means it breaks rather than bends. A hard hammer blow that would only flatten a lump of gold or lead shatters germanium into small pieces.

Silicon, the best-known metalloid, is shiny and brittle too, and it is found in sand and quartz. It is a semiconductor, a material in between for electricity: it carries electricity far less easily than copper but far more easily than glass, and adding tiny amounts of other elements changes how much it carries. With the right tiny additions, silicon can be made to carry electricity or to block it. A computer chip holds billions of tiny silicon switches, called transistors, that turn the flow of electricity on and off.
